title: Algorithms & Data Structures: Trees, Graphs and Hashes
welcome_lead: Step up to non-linear structures: trees, graphs and hash tables.
meta_desc: A-Level CS: binary trees, graph representations, hashing and traversal.
final_note: Non-linear structures unlock the real power of computer science.

concepts.def: A tree where each node has at most two children.
A set of vertices connected by edges, directed or undirected.
A structure mapping keys to values using a hash function.
Depth-first search — explores as deep as possible before backtracking.
Breadth-first search — explores all neighbours before going deeper.
When two keys hash to the same slot in a hash table.

walkthroughs.body_html: A binary search tree keeps left children smaller and right children larger than the parent. Lookup, insert and delete are O(log n) on a balanced tree, but degrade to O(n) on a skewed one.
DFS uses a stack (often the call stack via recursion) and dives deep. BFS uses a queue and explores level by level — useful for shortest-path on unweighted graphs.
A hash function turns a key into an index. Good hashes spread keys evenly. Collisions are handled by chaining (linked lists per bucket) or open addressing (probing for the next free slot).
